sentences.text: Hello and welcome to the NPTEL MOOC's course on Foundations for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems.
We will be continuing our discussion on resource optimization.

In particular, we are talking about resource optimization from the point of view of rendering, which is a very important component in any extended reality applications including virtual reality and augmented reality applications.
So, we will primarily focus on immersive experience, as we have already stated earlier, and we are going to relate the discussion to VR resource optimization in particular.

Although such concerns equally apply to AR, However, the emphasis is more on resource optimization in the context of VR because realistic scene generation is more important there and that requires more resources as compared to AR experiences.

In order to understand resource optimization concerns, we started our discussion on computer graphics, which deals with the rendering process, rendering on a computer screen or any display device such as HMDs.
So, we learned about the basic idea of computer graphics, including the 3D graphics pipeline stages.

Also, so far we have covered three of those stages, namely the first stage, object representation; the second stage, modeling transformation; and the third stage, lighting calculation or calculation of intensities at the pixel point pixel positions.
In this part of the lecture, we are going to talk about the fourth stage of the pipeline, that is, view transformation.
So, just to put things into perspective, we have this 3D graphics pipeline.
Now, here we have object representation, the first stage, which takes place in the local coordinate reference frame.
We already covered it.

Then we have modeling transformation, the second stage, also known as geometric transformation, which transfers the object definition from local coordinates to the definition in a world coordinate scene.
Then we have the third stage, that is lighting calculation, which as per our pipeline discussion, takes place in the world coordinate scene.
Now, this lighting calculation is quite complex, and we talked about one simple lighting model.
In this part, today's part of the lecture, we are going to cover the fourth stage, that is the viewing pipeline, comprising all these transformations and other processes.
And later on, we will cover the scan conversion.
So, let us get the idea of the fourth stage, that is view transformation.
Here again, our emphasis will be on giving you the basic idea rather than going into the intricate details.
So, we will try to confine our discussion to a bare minimum level.
So, what is the basic idea?
The idea is that when we see an image on a screen, any screen including HMD, we are basically seeing a projection of a portion of the 3D scene.
So, we have a 3D scene which we have constructed and illuminated with our earlier stages.

Now, when we say that we are trying to render it on a computer screen, then essentially what we are doing is Selecting a portion of it and then projecting it from a 3D scene to a 2D display plane or 2D view plane.
So, this is similar to taking a photograph.
So, if you are a photographer or if you know something about capturing photos, what do we do?
We typically have a camera.
Any camera, even your smartphone camera.
So, when we try to capture a photo, first we look at the scene with our naked eye; that is the 3D scene.
Then we look at the same scene using the camera screen.
Then we capture a portion of the scene.
So, the scene, our field of view covers a wide range of a wide portion of the scene.
However, we do not capture the entire thing; we capture only the portion which is within the field of view of the camera.
And we set the camera in such a way that our area of interest is captured.
Now, when we say captured, that means we are able to see it on our screen.
Now, the screen is a 2D plane, whereas the scene, the portion of the scene that we have captured, is in the 3D space.
So, then there is a transformation, a projection transformation, which transforms from 3D space to a 2D screen.
The same thing we try to simulate in computer graphics with a set of stages, which are the viewing pipeline stages.
So, view transformation essentially is this viewing pipeline.
It has its own sub-stages that simulate the process of capturing a photo.
So first, we do a viewing transformation, a 3D viewing transformation, where the 3D world coordinate description of the scene gets transformed to a 3D view coordinate description.
So we define a view coordinate system.
So, this is a 3D view coordinate.
So, we define a view coordinate system, then perform a transformation operation that transforms the 3D world coordinates into the view coordinate system.
Now, this is akin to saying that we are looking at the scene through the camera lens.
When we capture a photo, before that, we see the scene using the camera mechanism, the camera viewing mechanism provided.
So, looking at the scene through the camera viewing mechanism and looking at the scene through our naked eyes, these two are different things.

And when we are looking at the scene through the camera viewing mechanism, essentially the scene gets transformed from the world coordinate system to a view coordinate system that is defined by the camera or, in other words, the camera parameters.
So, that is what happens here.
The second thing is a projection transformation that projects the 3D view coordinate scene to a view plane, which is a 2D plane.
So, this is the projection transformation from the 3D view coordinate system to the 2D view coordinate system or 2D view plane.
And then finally, there is another transformation, which is the window-to-viewport transformation, that happens here.
Here, we transform from a 2D view plane description of the scene, or the projected scene, to a 2D device coordinate space.
Now, here, there are two more operations that take place: one is clipping, and one is hidden surface removal.
Clipping takes place in the 3D view coordinate system, as per our way of understanding the pipeline, and hidden surface removal again takes place in the 3D view coordinate system.
Just to emphasize here is that the way we are explaining the pipeline, it is not necessary that this sequence should be followed in implementation.
So, different implementations can alter the sequence of the stages or sub-stages.
So, this sequence of stages or sub-stages is not sacrosanct; it may be changed depending on the implementation.
So, we have three transformations: viewing transformation, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation; and two operations: clipping and hidden surface removal.
Together, they constitute the viewing pipeline.
That is the fourth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline.

So, in clipping, what happens is that we define a view volume; the objects that lie outside the view volume are removed or eliminated. Only the objects that are inside are retained.

roadmap.lecture_goal: master the principles of the 3D viewing pipeline to optimize VR resource rendering.

objectives.text: You'll be able to review the 3D graphics pipeline and understand how 3D scenes are projected onto 2D screens.
You'll be able to explain the stages of the 3D viewing pipeline, define projection types, and apply canonical view volumes.
You'll be able to describe the complete sequence of transformations from world space to the viewport and explain how clipping reduces computational complexity.

segments.subgoal: Review the 3D graphics pipeline stages and introduce the concept of view transformation

key_points.text: Resource optimization is particularly emphasized in VR because realistic scene generation requires more resources than AR experiences.
Computer graphics involves the rendering process onto a display device, such as an HMD.
Three stages of the 3D graphics pipeline have been covered: object representation, modeling transformation, and lighting calculation.
This lecture segment will focus on the fourth stage of the pipeline, which is view transformation.

key_terms.definition: Computer graphics deals with the rendering process, which is rendering on a computer screen or any display device such as HMDs.
Rendering is the process of rendering on a computer screen or any display device such as HMDs.
Object representation is the first stage of the pipeline that takes place in the local coordinate reference frame.
Modeling transformation is the second stage, which transfers the object definition from local coordinates to the definition in a world coordinate scene.
Lighting calculation is the third stage of the pipeline, which takes place in the world coordinate scene.
View transformation is the fourth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline.

segments.subgoal: Understand how 3D scenes are projected onto 2D screens via the viewing pipeline

key_points.text: The viewing pipeline is the fourth stage of the rendering process, comprising various transformations.
Rendering involves selecting a portion of the 3D scene and projecting it onto a 2D display plane.
The process of rendering is analogous to how a camera captures a portion of a 3D scene.
The fundamental task of the viewing pipeline is transforming data from 3D space into a 2D screen.

key_terms.definition: The viewing pipeline is the fourth stage of the lecture that comprises all the transformations and other processes used in rendering.
View transformation essentially is the viewing pipeline, which simulates the process of viewing a 3D scene on a screen.
Projection is the process of selecting a portion of a 3D scene and transforming it from 3D space onto a 2D display plane or view plane.
A projection transformation is the specific transformation that converts data from 3D space to a 2D screen.

segments.subgoal: Explain the stages and transformations of the 3D viewing pipeline

key_points.text: The viewing transformation converts 3D world coordinates into 3D view coordinates, simulating the scene through a camera lens.
The projection transformation converts the 3D view coordinate scene into a 2D view plane.
The window-to-viewport transformation maps the 2D view plane description to a 2D device coordinate space.
Clipping and hidden surface removal are operations that take place within the 3D view coordinate system.
The viewing pipeline consists of three transformations and two operations, but the sequence of these stages is not mandatory in implementation.

key_terms.definition: This transformation converts the 3D world coordinate description of the scene into a 3D view coordinate description.
This transformation projects the 3D view coordinate scene onto a view plane, which is a 2D plane.
This transformation converts a 2D view plane description of the scene into a 2D device coordinate space.
Clipping is an operation that takes place in the 3D view coordinate system.
Hidden surface removal is an operation that takes place in the 3D view coordinate system.
The viewing pipeline is constituted by the viewing transformation, projection transformation, window-to-viewport transformation, clipping, and hidden surface removal.

segments.subgoal: Explain the process of defining and executing the 3D viewing transformation

key_points.text: The 3D viewing transformation converts coordinates from a 3D world description to a 3D view coordinate description, simulating a camera view.
The view coordinate system is defined by camera parameters, including the camera position (origin), view point, and the look-at point.
The three mutually orthogonal axes (N, V, U) defining the view coordinate system are determined using vector operations like cross products.
The transformation from world to view coordinates is achieved through two basic operations: translation and rotation, combined into a composite matrix.

key_terms.definition: This transformation converts a description from a 3D world coordinate to a 3D view coordinate.
This is the reference frame within which all the scene points are defined.
This system has its own axes (u, n, and v) and is used to transfer a point from the world coordinate to the 3D view coordinate scene.
These are the three mutually orthogonal axes (N, V, and U) that together define the view coordinate system.
This matrix is the dot product of the rotation (R) and translation (T) transformation matrices.
The camera position serves as the origin vector with respect to the world coordinate scene.

segments.subgoal: Explain the differences between perspective and parallel projection methods

key_points.text: The view volume defines the portion of the scene to be projected, and objects outside this volume are discarded during the clipping process, which occurs before projection.
Perspective projection uses non-parallel projectors that converge to a center of projection, which provides a realistic rendering effect.
Parallel projection uses parallel projectors, meaning the center of projection is considered to be at infinity.
The required view volume shape depends on the projection type: a frustum for perspective projection, and a rectangular parallelepiped for parallel projection.

key_terms.definition: The view coordinate system is defined with respect to three camera parameters and is used to transform a point from the void coordinate system to the view coordinate system.
The view plane is typically defined as a rectangular area.
A 3D region in the scene that defines the portion of the scene that is going to be projected onto the view plane.
The process of discarding objects that are outside of the defined view volume but are part of the scene.
A type of projection where the projectors are parallel to each other, meaning the center of projection is at infinity.

segments.subgoal: Explain the concept of canonical view volumes and the procedures for parallel and perspective projections

key_points.text: The canonical view volume simplifies computationally intensive clipping operations by converting arbitrary view volumes into a normalized cube.
For parallel projection, the canonical view volume is obtained by scaling the arbitrarily defined view volume.
Projections are performed by multiplying point vectors in the 3D view coordinate system with the appropriate projection transformation matrix.
To convert the projected homogeneous coordinates into Cartesian points, the resulting coordinate values must be divided by the homogeneous factor (w).

key_terms.definition: A canonical view volume is a concept used to simplify pipeline computations.
It is a cube used to define the view volume, converting any arbitrary view volume into a standard shape.
For parallel projection, the canonical view volume is obtained by scaling the arbitrarily defined view volume.
This is a factor, typically not equal to 1, that requires division to convert the obtained coordinate values into Cartesian points.

segments.subgoal: Describe the sequence of transformations from world space to the final viewport

key_points.text: Projecting a point P involves transforming it through the view, canonical, and projection transformations (170-174).
The 'Window' is a normalized clipping window, while the 'Viewport' is a portion of the final screen defined in device space (181, 184).
The transformation from the window to the viewport maps an abstract representation to a device-specific representation (190).
The final Cartesian point is obtained by multiplying the window point by the transformation matrix and then dividing by the homogeneous factor W (203).

key_terms.definition: A window is the same as a normalized clipping window and is an abstract intermediate representation.
The viewport is defined in device space as a portion of the final screen where the scene will be rendered, specified by the screen or display origin and screen dimensions.
The view volume in which the point lies is transformed to a canonical view volume, which is typically the case before clipping.

segments.subgoal: Explain how clipping and hidden surface removal reduce computational complexity in rendering

key_points.text: Clipping removes objects that lie outside the defined view volume, retaining only those inside.
Clipping is performed before projection to ensure projection operations are applied to fewer vertices, thereby reducing computational complexity.
Hidden surface removal identifies and eliminates surfaces that are inside the view volume but are not visible due to occlusion by other objects.

summary.recap: The lecture covered two operations within the viewing transformation stage: clipping and hidden surface removal. Clipping eliminates objects that fall outside the defined view volume, while hidden surface removal removes surfaces that are not visible to the viewer, even if they are within the view. Both processes are performed to reduce the overall computational complexity before the scene is rendered.

open_questions.prompt: Explain the complete sequence of transformations required to map a point from the original world coordinate system to its final location on the display screen.
open_questions.reference_answer: A point first moves from the world coordinate system through several transformations to reach the 2D view plane. This process involves transforming the point to the view coordinate system, then to a canonical view volume, and finally projecting it onto the view plane using a projection transformation. Next, the point on the abstract normalized clipping window must be mapped to the device-specific viewport. This mapping uses a transformation matrix, which incorporates scaling and translation based on the window and viewport dimensions. Finally, the homogeneous coordinates are converted back to Cartesian points by dividing by the homogeneous factor W.

open_questions.prompt: Explain the fundamental differences between perspective and parallel projection, detailing how their mechanics affect the shape of the view volume and the resulting visual effect.
open_questions.reference_answer: Perspective projection utilizes projectors that converge to a center of projection, which is what gives us realistic rendering and a realistic feeling. In contrast, parallel projection uses projectors that are parallel to each other, meaning the center of projection is at infinity and the lines never meet. Consequently, the view volume for perspective projection takes the shape of a frustum. For parallel projection, the required view volume is a rectangular parallelepiped-shaped region.

open_questions.prompt: Explain the main idea of the 3D viewing transformation to a classmate who missed the lecture.
open_questions.reference_answer: The 3D viewing transformation converts a world coordinate description into a view coordinate description, simulating how a camera captures a scene. This process requires defining the view coordinate system using camera parameters, such as the camera position, view point, and look-at point. To set up these coordinates, we determine three mutually orthogonal axes: N, V, and U. Finally, the transformation from world to view is achieved by applying two basic operations—translation and rotation—using a composite transformation matrix.

open_questions.prompt: Explain the main ideas of clipping and hidden surface removal in the context of VR resource optimization to a classmate who missed the lecture.
open_questions.reference_answer: Clipping is a process where a view volume is defined, and any objects or parts of objects that lie outside this volume are removed. This operation is performed before projection so that the projection operations only need to be applied to a fewer number of vertices, which diminishes computational complexity. Hidden surface removal is another operation that addresses objects inside the view volume that are not visible to the viewer due to occlusion. By identifying and eliminating these non-visible surfaces, we further reduce computational complexity, which is essential for both realistic image generation and efficient rendering.
